Trump’s $1.2 trillion election dividend is desperate and dangerous

2026-09-11

President Trump is at it again, making big time promises without thinking through their ramifications. At the Republican convention that just concluded in Dallas, Trump said that every adult U.S. citizen would collect a cool five thousand bucks if Republicans hold both chambers of Congress.

The announcement is astounding, audacious and altogether crazy.

For one thing, I wonder if at some point in the lead-up to his promise Trump and his gang of sycophants actually took out a calculator and figured how much it would cost.

The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget did just that and came up with $1.2 trillion,which is about 3.5% of our country’s GDP.

That’s just plain crazy. CRFB notes that “this proposal is fiscally dangerous, economically backwards, and fundamentally unserious.”

That’s putting it mildly compared to my take, which is so crowded with expletives that I can’t, in deference to good taste, post them here.

More to the civilized  point is the fact that Trump has already promised dividends that he has yet to pay out. The guy’s a welsher.

  • Tariff dividends that he promised last year have yet to be paid.

  • DOGE dividends from cash saved by the budget cutting frenzy early on in his administration haven’t materialized.

  • Dividends are supposed to accrue from expiring ACA subsidies. Though still in its larval stage, I’m dubious about this promise, considering his track record.

Given the huge hole in our federal budget, it’s hard to see how any of those dividends will ever get paid. I wonder if anybody listening to Trump’s attempt at election bribery actually believes he'll come across this time.

The fiscal damage that the payout would cause is hard to overstate. I haven’t found a supportive economist to weigh in on this looney-tunes proposal. All I’ve found are harsh critiques.

Those critiques focus on the fiscal madness of further increasing our national debt and the inflation that would result from the $1.2 trillion that would suddenly be injected into our economy.

Trump’s promise isn’t just dangerous demagoguery. It’s irrational and illusional.

The GOP hasn’t got much to brag about on the policy front. If it has to resort to bribery as a means of propping up support, Republicans are in sad shape.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via Market Place Tech Report

How financial advisors for couples can get the “silent partner” involved

2026-09-10, updated: 2026-09-11

Over 40-plus years in financial planning, I noticed a common pattern with client couples: in meetings with advisors, one partner usually does most of the talking. The other sits back, nods in the right places, and answers direct questions. The professionals in the room key off the partner who talks. That's a natural response. It’s efficient. It also helps keep one spouse ignorant around the family finances.

How can planners help change the “silent partner” dynamic? I learned the value of actively bringing the quieter partner into the conversation by turning toward them, making eye contact, and asking for their thoughts. Even if the answer is still a shrug, the question signals that their view belongs in the conversation.

It also helps to suspend judgment and gently explore why someone is reluctant to participate. They may feel less “qualified” if they earn less than their partner. They may be afraid of looking foolish in front of two people who understand something they do not.

Many couples divide up the money work. Most of the time it doesn’t matter who manages the bills, tracks account balances, or does the tax returns. The arrangement turns risky when one partner doesn’t know enough about the finances. That lack of involvement can have serious consequences.

One concern is that eventually one partner will almost certainly need to handle the money alone as a result of death, divorce, or incapacity. I have sat with surviving spouses needing to learn everything about their finances at the worst possible moment. A few could not even name the bank that held their checking account.

Sometimes a partner is shut out on purpose. The National Network to End Domestic Violence reports that financial abuse occurs in 99 percent of domestic violence cases. For an abuser, keeping a partner ignorant about family finances is a way to control them and limit their options.

For planners, disregarding a silent partner also raises a question of ethics. A planner in a financial therapy study group I take part in described one client couple who were spending past their income and carrying a burden of debt. The husband handled their finances, knew how bad things were, and was communicating with the planner. The wife didn’t come to meetings, appeared to have no idea, and kept on spending. The planner realized she had become complicit in a destructive pattern of secret-keeping.

Joy Slabaugh, a Certified Financial Planner™ and licensed therapist who taught advisors to recognize financial abuse at this year's Financial Planning Association NorCal conference, offers a practical approach. Couple counselors commonly work under a stated policy that they will not hold a secret from one partner on behalf of the other. She recommends that planners do something similar, writing into the client agreement that they will meet individually with each partner on a set schedule.

Her recommendation was new to me, and it makes sense. It helps advisors maintain their clarity about representing both partners. It gives a partner who is used to staying in the background a chance to be heard without having to initiate a separate meeting. Also, if either partner strongly opposes the idea, that reaction is important information.

I have written before about the qualities to look for in an advisor who works well with couples. It would be worthwhile to also ask whether the firm will meet with each of you separately. One solo conversation a year would help give the silent partner a voice. It would help both the couple and the advisor to remember that, no matter who handles the accounts or earns the most money, the partners are equals in the financial planning relationship.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

via Floodlight

Let SNAP users buy what they want. We don’t need a nanny state

2026-09-09, updated: 2026-09-11

Cory Heidelberger just posted a piece in Dakota Free Press about how South Dakota retailers are uneasy about this year’s implementation of a bill that would deny sales of soft drinks to SNAP users in our grocery stores. SNAP stands for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, once familiarly known as “food stamps.”

Denying SNAP users access to soft drinks in the name of improving diets lends itself to a collectively smug sense of noblesse oblige, but it incurs some practical challenges for the food industry, particularly if the trend toward eliminating “junk food” from a SNAP purchaser's grocery cart spilled over (as it has in Texas, where the photo above was taken) to other products in South Dakota.

On the retail front, the new regulation is likely to cause some confusion in grocery stores throughout our state. Heidelberger’s piece notes that its implementation will create some administrative chaos, both within the private and public sectors as retailers and civil authorities debate and classify which products are or are not soft drinks.

On a broader scale, if food purchases are further restricted, retailers will have a long list of issues that they’ll have to deal with. First off, how do we come to a common definition of “junk food?” The concept is subjective and vague. I haven’t been able to find a universally recognized, scientifically based definition.

More difficult to quantify are the social effects of telling people how to spend the money they get from the state. Free choice is perhaps the essence of a democratic society. Does singling out a particular class of residents and denying them free choice at the food store extend the liberties that we cherish as Americans?  Of course not.  It stigmatizes and alienates people who have been taught early on that their access to some food items is restricted.

Think about kids from poor families who are old enough to figure out what’s going on. While grocery shopping with their families, a sign like the one above cuts them off from the aisle where all the treats are. Their more well-off schoolmates can buy that stuff at will, but they can’t. Could there be a more painful sense of exclusion?

Food choice restrictions based on income are an affront to human dignity and may do more harm than good.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via Institute of Local Self-Reliance

A farewell to Gloria Steinem. She helped make me a better man

2026-09-08, updated: 2026-09-11

My father may have been, overall, a product of his times, but he was also a free thinker. In those days, the 1930’s and 40’s, that was a bit radical. A free thinker was regarded in those days as an apolitical agnostic, so he kept it all to himself.

Except for the woman who married him and the way he raised his children.

He must have told me several times, since I have the clear recollection of him saying to me, “Boy, you could have been born anyone, anywhere. Never forget that. Thank your lucky stars you’re here.”

So my progressive outlook on life had begun quite early. My older sister, probably enabled by the free thinkers that were our parents, seriously lamented the fact of her birth as a female since, growing up in the 1950’s, she faced the limitations of powerful societal sexism. Smarter than most others, she still faced roadblocks everywhere. Besides stealing her birthday six years later, I also gained the fate of being born male. She never forgave me for either.

All of us were shocked when our dad told her, just prior to her leaving for college, that her primary duty in going to college was to find a good husband. His free thinking faltered now and again to the exigencies of socialization. Even our mother was appalled.

So it was not my father, but my sister who began me on the road towards feminism. And it was Gloria Steinem who put me firmly there.

Ten years prior to the time I was taking a Women’s Sex Roles course at the University of Iowa (my major was General Studies), Gloria Steinem was ghosting as a Playboy Bunny, and had written an expose that put her on the map. In 1973, she had just begun Ms. magazine with several others and was loudly celebrating the newly established Roe vs. Wade decision.

I was a post -Vietnam Vet and already had a failed marriage under my belt, due in large part to my own baked-in chauvinism, so the best part of me recognized that I needed to change, to grow. That Sex Roles course began to open my eyes. An essay was shared with three control groups… the same essay was given with a man’s name attached, a woman’s name attached, and no name at all. Even the women rated the woman’s essay lowest!

So I began listening in earnest to Gloria Steinem who eventually helped me become a better feminist than most women I have known.

There remains much work to do. The gender pay gap is 81 cents for women, a dollar for men. Child care remains an afterthought to our still male dominated legislatures.

Misogyny thrives in our White House. Those legislatures have made it more difficult for women to control their own futures and bodies.

Hail to Gloria Steinem. We must continue to speak her truths and continue her fight for equality.

Her history is a wealth of great quotes. She said women tend to be conservative in youth and get more radical as they get older because they lose power with age.

So if a young woman is not a feminist, I say, “just wait.”

Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years.

Catch the color and character of S.D. by using Hwy 44 instead of I-90

2026-09-07, updated: 2026-09-11

One of the major accomplishments of the Eisenhower administration in the 1950's was the creation and funding of the Interstate Highway System, which connects all 48 contiguous states into a network that promotes fast and efficient travel across our country.

In the postwar era, the Interstates quickly replaced railroads as America's preferred means of transportation. Middle-class American families discovered the joy and ease of road trips, and a culture grew up around these four lane highways that allow cars and semi trucks to move efficiently to thousands of destinations.

Here in South Dakota, Interstate 90 helped tourism to advance to a whole new level. Millions of visitors from states to the east of us are able to travel across our great state, stopping to see Mount Rushmore (and maybe even the Badlands) on their way to Yellowstone and other major attractions to the west. I-90 is a major national artery that crosses the country from Boston to Seattle, and our state is an integral part of it.

But maybe there's a downside to this efficient mode of transportation. In general, Interstates flatten out the terrain, and after a while everything looks the same. A network of truck stops, giant gas stations and convenience stores spring up at most exits, and suburban developments stretch out of cities (including Sioux Falls and Rapid City) as the Interstate provides a quick commute to work.

If you travel across South Dakota on a regular basis, you may have grown weary of I-90 and the predictable journey of 340 miles between our two major cities. How many times do you have to see the same billboards, promoting Wall Drug and the Firehouse Brewing Company?

Of course, the journey across the state on I-90 does have its moments. Crossing the Missouri River at Chamberlain offers a dramatic view, which has been heightened by Dale Lamphere's iconic Dignity Statue at the roadside rest area. Visitors who have not been here frequently are appropriately impressed. If they don't have time to drive through Badlands National Park and truly appreciate its magnificent scenery, they can at least catch a glimpse of the Badlands to the south as they cruise by at 80 miles per hour.

It's worth pointing out that there is an alternative route across South Dakota, and that is State Highway 44. If you're traveling west from Sioux Falls, you can take Interstate 29 south, and get off at either exit 64 or 68 and come west through the town of Lennox. At that point, get on Highway 44 and prepare yourself for a treat. This two-lane road will take you clear across the state, going through P-towns (Parker, Parkston, Platte) east of the river and W-towns (Winner, Witten, Wood, White RIver, Wanblee) west of the river.

If you are coming east from Rapid City, just go out to the airport and keep on going, following Highway 44 all the way east. Yes, these communities have gas stations and cafes in case you get hungry or your gas tank gets low. As you get out into the Pine Ridge reservation, you will enjoy spectacular Badlands scenery.

The Missouri River crossing on the Platte-Winner bridge is at least as intriguing as its I-90 counterpart, and you will also enjoy crossing the Vermillion, James, Little White, White and Cheyenne Rivers and seeing the natural terrain. There will be considerably less traffic than on the Interstate. The physical features along your journey will be more spectacular, and easier to contemplate and enjoy.

If you're not in a huge hurry, you will probably conclude that the scenic and more relaxed journey is well worth the extra 90 minutes that you spent coming across South Dakota.

Jay Davis is a retired Rapid City attorney

Photo: Interior, SD. The structure is roughly a century old, public domain, wikimedia commons

Reconstructing Hwy 85 will destabilize forest’s delicate balances

2026-09-05, updated: 2026-09-11

Editor’s note: this is an open letter, meant as a public comment , to Mark Malone, project manager at the South Dakota Department of Transportation

Good morning, Mr. Malone,

I just wanted to let you know that I oppose DOT’s current plan to reconstruct Highway 85 from Cheyenne Crossing to the Wyoming line. I’m 82, grew up in Lead, and all my life I’ve returned to that stretch of road, with its pristine, mostly untouched, clear-running stream, its splendid riparian zone and the marvelously varied terrain that stretches all the way from Cheyenne Crossing to the Wyoming line. It’s a rare place of serene and primitive beauty that (ironically!) has a highway running through it. Designed with a modicum of respect for the fragile environment it passes through, the highway, as it is, achieves a delicate symbiosis between the modern and the aboriginal—an odd entanglement that both sides have gotten used to. Straightening and broadening it will unfairly destabilize this delicate balance in favor of faster, but not necessarily safer, passage to more raucous places, like Roughlock Falls and Lead and Deadwood.

As currently planned, reconstruction will disrupt the basic ecology of a quieter and more subtle dimension of the Black Hills in favor of louder, and yes, let’s say it, more profitable destinations. But, for so many, the true destination, the real beauty of the Black Hills, is in its tranquil interstices, like those found along Highway 85. These places of rejuvenation are dwindling now as human activity advances. Yet, as obscured as they’ve become, when we do find them, they offer the rich and elusive gifts of the geological ages, gifts that speak in whispers and in the figures of their own language. One slows down and grows quiet in order to apprehend them. They are of another order and need unique advocates, since those on the fast and noisy side have already captured more than their share of the Hills. My request to DOT is that it take time to attend to the voices on nature’s side. Consider repairing the highway as it is, make some non-intrusive safety adjustments where needed, but take no more from the natural order than is warranted. Continue to protect and nurture the priceless side of the Highway 85 experience. Do that and you’ll have the profound thanks of a multitude of people who live and work here or come to visit.

Respectfully,  Harold Storsve

Harold Storsve is a native of the Black Hills, born and raised in Lead, South Dakota. For over 50 years, he worked as an antipoverty professional throughout the Western United States. Over the years he has also participated in local efforts to protect the natural integrity of the Black Hills, most notably during the Northern Hills heap leach gold mining surge of the 80s and 90s. He currently resides in Interior, South Dakota.

Knobe: Here is my view of the election from the cheap seats

2026-09-04, updated: 2026-09-11

Based on the primary and run-off Republican vote results, about 30% of South Dakota Republicans are hyper MAGA. They support Trump and are in his cult/gang.

70% of Rs might be some level of MAGA.

Of that 70% I’m guessing at about half of them are still regular Republicans. They support the policies of the party from 15 years ago. Not the current ones. They are struggling between “Party Loyalty” and good policy and common sense. None are speaking out publicly. It is quiet struggling.

Based on other states primary elections it is obvious that many Rs are NOT in lock step with MAGA.

I have no strong prediction on November election results. It is possible Brian Bengs will replace Mike Rounds in the U.S. Senate. The race is now tied. Mike has been making a lot of noise recently. The Republicans I associate with are not impressed. One asked, “Where has he been hiding the past 18 months?”

I have no strong sense on the U.S. House race. I do wonder if the picture of our Attorney General, the R candidate with Donald Trump both giving the “Thumbs Up” gesture will have an impact on the 50% of Regular Republicans. That picture shows strong Hyper MAGA loyalty.

Our current R Governor clobbered the Super MAGA candidate in the run-off election.  71 to 29%. However, the current Governor has publicly stated his support for Trump and has said former Governor Kristi Noem was a good governor. He is obviously MAGA. Not surprising party/cult/gang loyalty. Maybe bad reality politics.

I haven’t seen any polling, but the Non-Republican Candidate for Secretary of State, seems to be gathering good traction over his Trump/MAGA/cult/gang supporting opponent.

I have no sense on legislative races. I have visited with two Non-Republicans running in Districts in Sioux Falls. Smart people. Both young. Maybe a move towards Non-Republicans winning.

At the Minnehaha County Commission level, there are three Rs, a D, and an Independent seeking three seats. The D and Independent have both served on the Sioux Falls City Council. Goth have a good track record.  Both well known. It will be interesting to see if R party/cult/gang loyalty retails.

The game moves into the fourth quarter after Labor Day. Expect surprises and tricks. Maybe some skullduggery.

That’s my view of the game from the cheap seats.

Rick Knobe is a former mayor of Sioux Falls and radio talk show host, now retired.

via Electrek Feed

Cattle prices are taking a seismic drop. Trump’s policies aren’t helping any

2026-09-03, updated: 2026-09-11

Cattle markets have been getting hammered in recent months, largely because Trump’s tariff and trade policies create uncertainties that are overwhelming the market.  Nobody really seems to know what the heck is going on.

The magnitude of this drop ( 15% to 20% since last Spring) during a period of tight supplies is contra-intuitional, if not altogether crazy. [USDA](https://Beef Cows and Calf Crop) says that 2025’s beef cow and calf crop inventories are the lowest since 1961. So why are the markets selling off?

Farm Progress ticks off the itemized run of news that has led to this history-making episode in our live cattle markets:

  • Trump’s recent headline-grabbing announcement that he’s exempting tariffs on 300 tons of imported ground beef

  • Tyson’s closure of its Joslin, Illinois and Eagle Mountain, Utah, beef processing plants

  • Re-opening of the Mexican border for live cattle crossings

  • Worsening drought in the Southern Plains and the Southeast

July’s Cattle Inventory report from USDA showed that the country’s herd size has stabilized somewhat after steadily downtrending in recent years, but total numbers are still historically low, with USDA noting that “reduced feeder cattle numbers ultimately imply limited future fed cattle supplies, which should provide some support to cattle prices.”

So where’s the support?

None of the supply/demand numbers in the report justify the sharpness of the drop in live cattle prices. To me that suggests the markets are looking ahead to a supply increase that will have to come from somewhere other than domestic producers.

Farm Progress pins the negative price sentiments directly to Trump’s beef import plans, pointing specifically to the opening of the border to feeder cattle imports. Given the political environment as midterms approach and the overall sensitivity to high food prices that must be making Republicans nervous as voting nears, it makes sense to expect price-reducing policies to come out of Washington for a while.

Are South Dakota’s congressional delegates going to bat for our state’s cattle producers on this? They’re giving it some lip service, but so far the responses from Sens. Thune and Rounds are tepid at best. Outgoing Rep. Dusty Johnson says he has “raised concerns” with the White House, but I imagine that his lame-duck status has rendered him politically irrelevant at this point.

As to consumers, we’ll have to wait a bit to see if the cattle market selloff translates into cheaper prices for beef. Numbers from July indicate that ground beef prices, averaging $6.89 per pound, are 10% higher than they were last year. I’m guessing a price drop, if any, will be marginal because the live animal is just a fraction of the price we pay at the grocery store.

Trump’s flailing efforts to get consumer prices down will probably come up short again.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. A Vietnam vet ponders Iran, presidential lies and the People’s Republic

2026-09-02, updated: 2026-09-11

I was on the front lines of a war that outlived expectations. Our incursion into Vietnam was planned to be short and decisive. Our intervention was intended to be limited. Our display of military might was supposed to stabilize the regime we supported. Our enemies were expected to quickly back down and negotiate.

The war was supposed to be this and supposed to do that and so on and so forth, but as it turned out, the “this and that,” whatever they were expected to be, never materialized. As to “so on and so forth?” It turned out to be a decade of wasted blood, a sense of futility that was reflected in our grunt lingo. When one of us was killed we said “he got wasted.”

What happened is this: We met up with a small, determined enemy that got support from a powerful ally named China … and it took us more than a decade to extract ourselves from that tangled mess. We accomplished nothing. Our adversaries took over the entire country.

American hubris turned into American humble pie.

As I review the flashbacks I still get from Vietnam, what keeps coming back to me isn’t just the war that was in front of my face. What I also get is a strong sense of China’s presence.

It was plenty obvious during my war that support from what was then called Red China was a major, possibly decisive, factor in keeping our enemies in North Vietnam intact and persistently on the offensive. Chinese armaments kept the North Vietnamese afloat.

I know something about those armaments. I was on the receiving end of countless Chinese 107 mm. rocket attacks, and the enemy never seemed to run out of them.

I doubt that the Chinese will become such conspicuously involved military supporters of Iran during this latest American attempt at imposing our will on a region that’s on the other side of the globe.

I do think that China will become a factor by supporting Iran economically, which in its way could be just as effective a support mechanism as the arms that China’s forebears supplied to North Vietnam.

The Brookings Institution has done a study on this, concluding that China has benefitted from the U.S.-Iran war. Nobel Laureate Paul Krugman recently published a piece titled How China Won the Iran War. There are those who disagree, but I have to lean with those who see the war in Iran as a net positive for China, if only because the U.S. has lost a lot of good will over this ill-advised venture that seems like it will fester for a while.

Trump’s pathetically poor prognostication that the war will end in a matter of weeks has taken its place alongside some of his other monumentally fatuous claims ( prices will come down on day one, tariffs are paid by foreigners, the national debt will be reduced).

Unlike Vietnam, Trump’s war may eventually end before it sinks into a quagmire, but the lying? It will be an indelible part of the Iran war’s history … same as it was in Vietnam.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via Sacramento Bee

How will a declining population affect your Social Security

2026-09-01, updated: 2026-09-11

If you are under 50, will Social Security still be there when you retire?

The answer starts with a number, 2.1, that demographers call the replacement rate. When women have an average of about 2.1 children, a country’s population stays level. Below that, without immigration, the population shrinks.

The fertility rate in the United States was 1.599 in 2024 and stayed near 1.6 last year, a record low. The last time this country reached replacement level was 2007.

Nearly every wealthy country is in the same position. China and Singapore are at 1.0. Japan and Spain are at 1.1, Italy at 1.2, Canada at 1.3, Germany at 1.4, and Britain and France at 1.6. South Korea holds the world record at 0.7.

Wealth, education, health care, and paid work for women all correlate with smaller families. High birth rates now cluster in the poorest countries or the poorest areas of prosperous countries. Somalia, Chad, the Central African Republic, and Niger all run near 6.0.

The world population, now roughly 8.3 billion, is still growing by about 69 million people a year. That works out to 0.84 percent annually, down from more than 2 percent in the 1960s. The United Nations projects the total will peak near 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s and decline slowly after that.

What does this have to do with Social Security? It is largely a pay-as-you-go system. Taxes withheld from people’s paychecks this month pay much of this month's benefit checks. There is no account somewhere with your name on it. The program was built in 1935 around a population with far more workers than retirees, and those retirees did not collect for long. A man who reached 65 in 1960 could expect to live to about 80. Today he can expect to live to 85.

In 1950 there were 16.5 workers paying in for every person collecting. Today there are about 2.7, a number that the Social Security trustees expect to drop closer to two by 2040. By 2030, for the first time, Americans over 65 will outnumber those under 18.

Immigration is the one factor that changes this arithmetic quickly. The Census Bureau projects that deaths in this country will exceed births by around 2038. From that point forward, under current projections, immigration becomes the only source of population growth.

This does not mean Social Security disappears. I have written before about the alarmist coverage of the trustees' reports. The program will be adjusted instead, through some combination of higher payroll taxes, later retirement ages, and slower benefit growth. Even if Congress never acts, incoming payroll taxes would still cover roughly 80 percent of scheduled benefits.

There is a reasonable argument that population decline is not a catastrophe. Fewer people means less pressure on housing, energy, and food. Automation may cover some of the missing labor, and countries have absorbed demographic shifts before. Those adjustments take decades, though, and you will likely retire before they finish.

The bigger short-term impact is likely to be the cost of aging. Home health aides, nursing staff, and skilled trades come out of the same shrinking pool of working-age people. Fewer workers competing for those jobs means higher wages, which means higher prices for the care you may need in your eighties.

If you are under 50, here is my view: Yes, Social Security will be there. And it will probably pay you less than your statement projects. It’s wise to assume long-term care will also cost more than today's estimates. Base your retirement saving and planning on the assumption that you will fund more of your own old age than your parents had to.

via Market Place Morning Report

Grain and soybean prices move higher as war slows shipping in Black Sea

2026-08-31, updated: 2026-09-11

American grain and soybean farmers got a sharp price move to the upside in recent days as the Russia/Ukraine war is moving one of its flash points to ports on the Black Sea.  A large source of the world’s wheat, around 25%, and corn, about 10%, pass through the port of Odessa, so a stoppage there, combined with an exceptionally low wheat harvest in the United States, has caused grain futures prices to skyrocket.

The timing might be short-lived, but it has been financially fortuitous even as it springs from carnage and destruction. Blood money it may be, but it’s money nonetheless.

And our farmers can use the help.

Trump’s bungling trade policies have been hurting American food producers for the past couple of years, both in lowering prices for their products and raising prices for one of their most important inputs, fertilizer. This “relief rally” has given farmers some financial breathing room, especially as harvest season approaches.

But, as nice a turn of financial events as this has been, it’s useful to remember an all-important aspect of the situation: This is a wartime dislocation and it’s causing distorted prices. A significant pullback of the fighting in the Black Sea could move prices lower as quickly as it raised them.

Shrewd farmers are using this rally to lock in the most favorable prices they’ve seen in years, knowing full well that once the fireworks are over in Odessa, Trump’s same ol’, same ol’ trade and tariff policies will still be in effect.

As to the other negative result of Trump’s farmer-unfriendly trade policies, namely the high cost of inputs, not much is likely to be changed by the warfare in the Black Sea. Fuel, fertilizer and equipment prices will remain high thanks to the war in Iran.

As an old grain and livestock trader (I traded and brokered ag commodities in Rapid City for a decade, following a decade I spent on the trading floors in Chicago, where I focused on derivatives) it’s great to see some of the best prices in years getting posted on the commodity boards. And, yes, as an old grain and livestock trader, I also know that good times are usually fleeting. It’s important to remember that nothing has changed in terms of supply/demand fundamentals. Wartime shipping disruptions are causing the market spike, and they can end as quickly as they started.

I’m glad that financially stretched farmers, who’ve been supported by cash payouts to offset the disastrous financial effects of Trump’s policies, are getting this chance to seize a moment and hope that they’ll use their marketing judgement to lock in some of these gains.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via Sacramento Bee

South Dakota should use AI to strengthen apprenticeship programs

2026-08-28, updated: 2026-09-11

South Dakota is deciding what skills its workforce needs next. The Workforce Development Council’s August 25 agenda included an Essential Skills Certificate, Hot Careers and new career-and-technical-education standards. That is exactly the right moment to decide what happens when artificial intelligence takes over the routine work through which young employees once learned a job.

The newest Stanford Digital Economy Lab employment analysis raises the stakes. Using ADP payroll data covering millions of U.S. workers through June 2026, the researchers found employment among workers ages 22 to 25 in highly AI-exposed occupations about 19 percent below where it would be if it had kept pace with similarly aged workers in less-exposed occupations. The comparable gap was 15 percent in the July 2025 data vintage. The adjustment appears mainly through reduced hiring rather than higher separations, and experienced workers show no comparable gap.

South Dakota employers should respond by redesigning entry-level work before deleting it.

The state already has a useful model. Registered apprenticeship in South Dakota combines paid work with structured training and lets employers build programs around the skills their jobs actually require. AI should extend that logic into offices, professional services, health administration, finance, agriculture, manufacturing support and other knowledge-intensive work.

Start with the task map. Let AI handle routine preparation: first drafts, basic research, scheduling, standard summaries, document formatting and predictable data pulls. Then move junior employees sooner into work that develops judgment: verifying an output against source material, spotting an exception, testing a recommendation, asking a customer the clarifying question, explaining a decision and escalating the case that does not fit the template.

Next, make coaching a measured production activity. If AI saves a team 10 hours of preparation each week, assign a portion of those hours to senior review. Give experienced employees responsibility for showing new hires how they distinguish a plausible answer from a reliable one, how they recognize an unusual case and how they communicate uncertainty without freezing a decision.

Finally, add one workforce metric to every AI project: time to independent competence. Cost, hours and output still matter. They do not tell leaders whether the organization is building the next generation of people who can handle the hard cases. A company that cuts junior labor today and discovers three years later that nobody learned the work has booked a short-term saving and created a long-term capability deficit.

South Dakota’s workforce strategy already recognizes that skills grow through work, standards and employer involvement. The AI era calls for the same discipline. Automate routine preparation, then use the resulting capacity to accelerate apprenticeship. The goal should be fewer wasted hours and faster development of people who can make sound decisions on their own.

Gleb Tsipursky, PhD, a behavioral scientist, is CEO of Disaster Avoidance Experts, and author of The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results (Georgetown University Press, 2026) .

“Stolen election 2020”. A historically blatant lie lives on.

2026-08-28, updated: 2026-09-11

﻿A few years ago I wrote a column asking this question:

If the 2020 election was “stolen”, why has nobody been arrested? That vast conspiracy would have required hundreds if not thousands of individuals committing federal election law felonies.

Now, here we are almost six years after the election. Still no charges. No arrests. Not even any specific accusations remaining after frivolous and bizarre attempts to get help from friendly judges failed.

This was either the most secretive conspiracy in history, or…it never happened.

Yet, administration officials still appear before congress and find it impossible to say five simple words:  “Joe Biden won the election.” Office holding Republicans either repeat the lie or misdirect the question.

The penalty for saying that, apparently, is banishment from MAGA.

Instead, these men and women choose to permanently stain themselves as pathetic bootlickers with no personal or professional integrity.

This “stolen election” fallacy will join other events in our history where ideas were proven to be misguided by facts and evidence. Here are a few random examples of counterfeit history:

  • Senator Joe McCarthy convinced millions of Americans there were hundreds of Communists in government. He never made his “lists” public and did not ever identify a single communist.

  • Over 12,000 accusations of “satanic ritual abuse” were lodged during the “Satanic Panic,” starting in the 1980’s, pushed by fundamentalist Christians, therapists, law enforcement agencies, and child advocates. Not a single charge was substantiated.

  • Also starting in the 1980’s media reports predicted a flood of mentally damaged “crack babies” would become a burden on society as they aged, and it became accepted as valid. Very small studies erroneously warned of this, but it proved to be a myth.

  • In the news now, “trans men becoming women” are threatening college and pro women’s basketball. There is no evidence of a single “trans” player in either group. None.

  • About 120,000 USA residents of Japanese descent were interred in camps in World War 2 under the presumption they would be loyal to Japan.  Although some real spies were operating outside, forcing those everyday folks into the camps was unnecessary and counterproductive to the war effort. No Japanese spies were ever found, tried, or convicted among the more than 120,000 Japanese Americans imprisoned in U.S. internment camps during World War II.

  • “Weapons of Mass Destruction” was a mistaken justification for invading IRAQ.  Both parties and the public overwhelmingly agreed. Now we know the evidence was thin and manufactured and, of course, no WMD was ever found.

  • The “Stolen Election” of 2020 will be regarded in history as self evidently bogus just like these examples. Even as time proved them wrong, very few individuals have apologized for the damage they caused by pushing these fictions. They remain shameless.

We have over a decade of examples proving MAGA has no shame ( “grab them by the p____!”), and they’ll likely not ever admit how wrong they have been.

Will we ever hear John Thune, Dusty Johnson, Mike Rounds and other elected republicans say this:  “Joe Biden won the 2020 election and we were wrong in not standing up for the truth when our leader demanded that we go along with the lie.”

No, not likely; they are too far into the tangled web.

Meanwhile, this perpetuation of counterfeit history is the platform for new claims of fraud sure to come in November.

Mike Levsen is a former mayor of Aberdeen

via Electrek Feed

Data centers need more examination, not reflexive rejection

2026-08-27, updated: 2026-09-11

I just got a press release that says 19 Democratic legislative candidates have taken the Data Center Accountability Pledge (D-CAP), committing themselves to taking action against data center expansion in South Dakota. You can find the signers in the link at the end of the pledge below. The letter itself was signed by Amanda Potter, running for the House of Representatives in District 9 (Sioux Falls/Hartford) and Jeff Shelton, running for the Senate in District 32 (Rapid City).

Here’s the letter:

Sioux Falls/Rapid City, SD – August 24, 2026 – A group of 19 legislative candidates from across South Dakota have formally signed the Data Center Accountability Pledge (D-CAP), committing to taking action on data center expansion in the state and pledging to protect “consumer, communities, and the environment” if elected into office.

“This pledge represents a meaningful commitment to action, not just rhetoric,” said Amanda Potter, South Dakota House of Representatives candidate from District 9 (western Sioux Falls and Hartford). “By signing it, these candidates are signaling that data centers will be one of their foremost priorities in the 2027 legislative session. Furthermore, we will make sure information about the actions we take during session is easily accessible by the average South Dakotan, not hidden away in the legislative record.”

Jeff Shelton, South Dakota Senate candidate from District 32 (north and central Rapid City), said, “Many of the candidates who have signed this pledge have spent the last several weeks knocking on doors and listening to voters in their communities. In these conversations with the neighbors and relatives we hope to represent, it’s clear that data centers aren’t wanted in South Dakota. If elected, we intend to show South Dakotans that we hear their message loud and clear. Through commitments ranging from legislation action to rejection of special interest money, we stand committed to protecting our constituents.”

Both Potter and Shelton encourage other candidates throughout the state, no matter the party, to sign the pledge and commit to voters that they will keep their best interests at the forefront. The key commitments of the pledge are:

● Day zero action: Candidates pledge to begin work on protections for South Dakotans and their communities immediately upon election, before the 2027 legislative session begins.

● Rejection of financial interests: Candidates pledge that they have rejected and will reject campaign donations or other support from groups aligned with data centers. Candidates will not support sales tax waivers or other tax incentives to promote data center construction.

● Ongoing transparency during session: Candidates will provide clear communication regarding any legislative action regarding data centers on the D-CAP website (www.dcapsd.org).

● Defense of local control: Candidates will oppose any bills that weaken local governments’ ability to regulate, pause or ban data center development in their own communities.

Read the D-CAP Pledge and review candidate signees here .

I’m neither categorically for nor against data centers, but the pledge’s commitment “to work on protections of South Dakotans and their communities immediately upon election” even before the legislative session begins in January suggests a sweeping, generalized hostility to data centers. That impression is supported by the release’s opening statement, in which the group commits itself “to taking action against data center expansion in South Dakota.”

I have to take exception to a broadside like that. I’ve done enough examination of the data center expansion issue to know that some have succeeded and that others are nothing but a headache. There are more than 2,000 data centers in the United States. Focusing on the failures and smearing the whole concept as a result is not sound leadership.

As far as our state is concerned, we certainly should examine and debate each project that comes calling. But “taking action” against “expansion” as a starting position? No way. That gives an impression of closed-mindedness, which is a bad message to send to the rest of the world and is not exactly what we want to see in the representatives we send to Pierre.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via Market Place Tech Report

Trump’s reckless trade war with Canada will hurt U.S. farmers

2026-08-26, updated: 2026-09-11

Here we go again.

As if American farmers haven’t already been punished enough by President Trump’s reckless trade wars, his latest skirmish with Canada will only add to the financial strain and frustration that has bedeviled America’s ag economy since Mr. “Art of the Deal” took office.

Trump is threatening to raise tariffs on vehicles, auto parts and steel coming into the U.S. Why? Trump says it’s because Canada isn’t cooperating in ongoing negotiations. Trump is so frustrated and angry that he plans to increase tariffs on Canadian imports by as much as 50%, which will likely make goods coming from our northern neighbor prohibitively expensive for many Americans.

The impulsive Trump apparently doesn’t have the patience to negotiate with Canada’s trade representatives and has decided to scare them into submission by imposing these punitive tariffs in January.

Trump’s “let’s scare the hell out of ‘em” ploy has so far failed. It certainly hasn’t worked on the combat front in Iran, and it hasn’t done much on the trade policy front, either. He promised to reduce our country’s negative trade balance but instead the U.S. trade deficit has been as large as ever since Trump took office in 2025.

As to the current flap, American farmers are about to get shafted by yet another trade policy flop. How? because Canadians are already retaliating against Trump’s hot-headed approach. They just imposed a sweeping series of tariffs on imported U.S. farm goods, starting on September 8.

Ag producers across the board will feel the new jump in tariffs on their Canadian sales. Aware of this, American Farm Bureau Federation Zippy Duvall told The Fence Post, “Canada has been one of the most important trading partners for U.S. agriculture since our first free trade agreement in 1989 … we are concerned … additional tariff escalations and subsequent retaliation will hurt U.S. agriculture at a time when farmers and ranchers are already struggling.”

The livestock trade has already rendered a snap opinion. Yesterday’s sharp selloff in cattle and hog futures at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange speak for the reception that the tariff news got on the trading floor.

But it doesn’t stop at ag.

Canada’s retaliatory response to Trump’s threats will rattle everybody, not just farmers and ranchers, involved in cross-border trading. The U.S. industrial sector is also going to feel the pressure. Nobody gets out of here unscathed. Both producers and consumers live in the limbo of Trump’s uncertainty and growing ineffectiveness. We all pay the price for Trump’s  volatile temperament and chronic miscalculations.

Canadians have some reason to call Trump’s bluff on this latest round of bravado. And Americans have some reason to be sick and tired of it.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via Market Place Tech Report

Stock market volatility? It’s in the eye of the beholder. Stay calm

2026-08-25, updated: 2026-09-11

On the last Wednesday in July, I got several phone calls from clients. On the last Friday in July, nobody called. Why the difference? On Wednesday, the S&P 500 dropped 1.52 percent and the Nasdaq composite dropped 1.74 percent. On Friday, the S&P 500 gained 0.7 percent and the Nasdaq gained 1 percent.

Plenty happened in between those two days. The Federal Reserve held rates steady and gave no guidance about what comes next. Major international companies reported earnings; one gained 15 percent and another lost 7 percent. Oil prices moved based on the war with Iran. All these events earned headlines. None of them changed where the month ended.

For the last week of July, the S&P 500 and the Dow each finished up about 1 percent. For the month, the S&P 500 finished down 0.1 percent and the Dow finished up 0.3 percent. A volatile month ended almost exactly where it started.

How volatile your portfolio feels depends mostly on how often you look at it. Daily prices jump around. Weekly prices jump less. Monthly prices are smoother than weekly, and annual prices are smoother than monthly. Checking more frequently does not change your investment. It does change your level of anxiety.

To understand this, think of the value of your house. Most people believe home values rise steadily along with inflation, and they believe it partly because nobody appraises a house every morning. If strangers knocked on your door each day with firm cash offers, you would watch your home value fluctuate the way your 401(k) does.

Frequent checking produces fear. Losing money feels considerably worse than gaining the same amount feels good, so every look at a falling balance registers as a small emergency. The more emergencies you live through, the more likely you are to act on one. I have seen clients sell because of a sudden drop and then spend two years waiting for a re-entry point that never felt safe enough.

Since 1980 the S&P 500 has fallen an average of 14.2 percent at some point during each calendar year, according to J.P. Morgan's Guide to the Markets. Annual returns were still positive in 35 of those 46 years.

Even the worst stretch on record is milder than most people assume. The weakest ten-year run for the S&P 500 in the modern era was 2000 through 2009. It included a 22.1 percent loss in 2002 and a 36.6 percent loss in 2008, yet the decade’s annualized loss was 0.95 percent. Investors who held through the two worst years came out roughly even after ten years.

The S&P 500 spent July going nowhere. Whether that month was calm or nerve-racking depended on how often you checked your portfolio. Over the years I’ve received plenty of client calls about dramatic daily market drops. I have never had a client call about a flat month.

So my suggestion is to look less often, even if you have to start gradually. Move from daily to weekly. When weekly stops bothering you, move to monthly by reading statements when you get them instead of logging in at other times. To make it easier, turn off price alerts on your phone and take brokerage apps off your home screen. This reduces opportunities to react.

I wrote several years ago that the only thing you can count on the stock market to do is fluctuate, and that the wisest response is usually to do nothing. Nothing in the past few weeks has changed my mind. Looking less often will not change your return. It will make you far less likely to damage the return you already have.

via Electrek Feed

Trump plan to import ground beef is more about baloney than beef

2026-08-24, updated: 2026-09-11

Cattle producers are fuming at President Trump's decision last week to bring 300 metric tons of ground beef into the country, tariff free. With cattle markets falling hard since the first of August, this added supply of foreign beef sends a negative signal to ranchers.

That doesn’t seem to bother Trump, who said he’s doing it “to substantially lower the price of ground beef for working American families.”

To that I’d say his expectations are unrealistic. He’s overstating the downside pricing effect of putting this relatively piddly amount of beef into the market.

First of all, how many pounds of beef are we talking about?  300 tons is 600,000 pounds, which sounds like a lot, but is actually a fraction of total beef consumption in the United States, where people eat about 28 billion pounds (roughly 14 million tons) of beef every year. That equates to 76 million pounds a day.

I don’t get where adding 600,000 pounds of imported beef to the supply chain will have much of an impact on prices at retail outlets and I doubt that it will. Trump is putting on a show, acting like he’s doing something about inflation. Substantive results won’t materialize.

Still, he’s determined to promote his fantasy, saying that “we have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices.”

Where those commitments come from and how they’ll be put into place is another story. I mean, where, when and how will this beef be segregated from higher priced domestic supplies, and who will be the consumers purchasing it?

More interesting though is that Trump is apparently requiring retailers to set their prices for this imported commodity. That’s a common tactic in controlled economies, and is also a classic example of how communism works, where prices are set by the authorities, not by the market. Since when does a Republican, and one who is lately using the word “communist” to describe  American Democrats, step into the market place to make sure goods are sold at a price determined by him?

That’s about as communist as it gets, isn’t it? Don’t know about you, but I can’t wait to sink my teeth into a “commie burger.” Karl Marx would approve.

In the meantime, cattle producers and their representatives in Congress are making a justified  fuss over the president’s decision. The amount may be negligible, but the precedent isn’t the most promising for the livestock industry.

Oh, and there’s one more thing.  Trump’s explanation that removing tariffs will cheapen beef is a tacit – no, a brazen – admission that despite his claims otherwise, tariffs actually do raise prices for consumers.

Trump and his misguided advisors must believe this move will give Trump some creds as an inflation fighter, but I doubt that people are buying it. This plan is more about baloney than beef.

via Sacramento Bee

Trump’s promise goes pfft. U.S. debt, now $40 trillion, is up, not down

2026-08-22, updated: 2026-09-11

This week’s announcement that our nation’s debt has surpassed $40 trillion should be received with a collective sense of disgust.

After his history of broken promises on this, there’s no point expecting President Trump to get involved. He pledged to start whittling down the debt once he took office in 2025. He made the same promise before he took office in 2016.

Did he deliver? Please. So far he’s delivered squat. The debt increased during both of his terms. He’s hopeless. I recently discussed Trump’s inauthenticity, a quality that has been exposed — no, highlighted — by the run-up of red ink that has taken place during his time in the White House.

Trump’s lack of success at reining in our nation’s debt after he promised unequivocally to do so may well be the most significant failure of his presidency.

How’s that? I’ll let Ben Tomchik, Vice President and Deputy Chief of Staff of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget explain the implications of all this. In an email titled “Three reasons to worry about rising Treasuries,” Tomchik’s organization writes:

Interest rates on U.S. Treasury bonds recently rose to levels not seen in decades. A recent 30-year Treasury auction ended with yields at over 5.2% – the highest at auction since 2001. Market yields rose further, reaching over 5.3% on August 17, the highest level since 2007. Analysts cite a variety of factors driving the rise, including economic fallout from the war in Iran, persistent inflation, competition for borrowing due to AI investment, and increasing federal budget deficits. The Congressional Budget Office recently raised its estimate of the FY 2026 deficit from $1.9 trillion to $2.1 trillion, with a $432 billion deficit in July alone.

Here are three reasons to worry about higher interest rates on Treasuries:

1) Higher Rates Harm Affordability

Treasury rates serve as the benchmark for borrowing throughout the economy. As Treasury rates rise, so too do the interest rates for home mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards. For example, 30-year mortgage rates recently rose to 6.7%, the highest in about a year. Rising borrowing costs discourage capital investment, harm small business formation, weaken housing affordability, and ultimately slow wage and economic growth. One of the best things policymakers could do to address affordability concerns is to reduce federal borrowing and put us on a path to achieve a 3% deficit-to-GDP target.

2) Government Interest Expense Grows Even Larger

Increased Treasury rates combined with historically high debt lead to skyrocketing interest costs for the federal government. Over $1 trillion will be spent this fiscal year on interest alone, with more than $16 trillion total projected over the coming decade. But if interest rates remain high this year and are 1 percentage point higher than projected over the next decade, it would add another $3.5 trillion to the debt. Interest is the fastest growing line item in the budget, and we’re spending more on interest than on defense or Medicaid. Every dollar spent on interest is one that cannot be used elsewhere, reducing flexibility for the government to respond to emerging threats and opportunities.

3) We Risk Entering a Debt Spiral

While no one knows when the actual debt “tipping point” will occur, one thing that becomes increasingly likely as rates rise is a potential debt spiral. This can occur when the average interest rate paid on debt is higher than the rate of economic growth. For most of the last 60 years, the interest rate has been below the economic growth rate except for brief periods of economic contraction. But since 2023, most new debt has been issued at rates above the expected long-term growth rate. Once the average interest rate on debt exceeds the growth rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio grows indefinitely – potentially leading to a fiscal crisis.

It’s clear that Trump is helpless to do anything about this. The nation’s soaring debt numbers have obliterated his promises to get our deficits under control.

So what to do about the situation? There are many options, but we need people who can exercise them. It would be helpful if we sent representatives to Washington who take the nation’s debt obligations more seriously than those who are there now. I’m sure most sitting representatives will contend that they do take the red ink seriously … but we don’t need them and their unfulfilled rhetoric. We need elected officials who take oversized debt seriously enough to actually do something about it.

via Sacramento Bee

If he wins the race, will Jackley be a rubber stamp for Trump?

2026-08-21, updated: 2026-09-11

South Dakota has a number of important statewide election contests this fall. Our new Governor, Larry Rhoden, won a surprising landslide in the Republican runoff election over Toby Doeden, the extreme right-wing multimillionaire who had come in first in the primary but failed to clear the 35% threshold required for victory.

Rhoden faces Democrat Dan Ahlers, a seasoned former legislator and Democratic Party leader who lost the U.S. Senate race to Mike Rounds back in 2020.

Rounds, who has supported virtually all of Donald Trump's policies, is seeking a third term in the Senate, but his only opponent is Brian Bengs, running as an Independent, now that the Democratic nominee, Julian Beaudion, withdrew from the race at the last possible minute.

Bengs was the Democratic candidate for Senate against John Thune in 2022, shortly after he moved to South Dakota, and changed his voter registration back to Independent within weeks after his loss. Bengs likes to point out that he worked briefly as a ranger at Wind Cave National Park and is currently living in a camper while he builds a house to live in.

Perhaps our most interesting statewide race is for U.S. Congress, since there is no incumbent running after Dusty Johnson finished a dismal third in the Republican primary for Governor. The Republicans nominated Marty Jackley, who has served as Attorney General and as U.S. Attorney over the years. Democrats are running Nikki Gronli, who made friends around the state when she served as our rural development director in the US Department of Agriculture, and has been campaigning tirelessly and holding town halls wherever people are willing to gather.

"Nikki G for SD", who stands barely five feet tall, has put forth a program that includes fighting the fertilizer industry and meatpackers who are strangling our beleaguered family farmers, opposition to federal tax breaks for AI data centers, standing up to Donald Trump's tariffs on necessary farm inputs, as well as making Obamacare affordable for working families, improving health care on our reservations and working closely with tribal colleges, supporting early childhood education (Pre-K), and investing in rural schools and in the Disabilities Education Act.

You could say that Gronli does not want to leave any South Dakotan behind. Her positions are somewhat reminiscent of the last Democrat to represent this state in Washington, Senator Tim Johnson, who was never flashy but also never lost an election.

For his part, Jackley has always been a competent attorney. He has managed to keep the Attorney General's office out of the headlines for most of his tenure.

It is interesting that Jackley would want to go to Washington at this point in his career. The overwhelming suspicion would be that Jackley will be yet another rubber stamp for Trump, supporting the directionless war against Iran and economic policies that favor billionaires and that prevent local communities from reining in (or even prohibiting) data centers in their midst.

If Jackley does not intend to serve as a Republican rubber stamp, he needs to explain convincingly where he will stand up for his constituents and eschew the party line. Otherwise, moderate Republican voters and many Independents may want to split their tickets and vote for Nikki Gronli.

Jay Davis is a retired Rapid City attorney
